---
title: "Tables"
---

Use `attaviz.table()` to create a publication table from a pandas DataFrame.
It supplies Attaviz typography, colors, alignment, and spacing, then returns a
native [Great Tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/) `GT` object.
Chain Great Tables methods to format values, rename columns, and add footnotes.

## Install table support

```bash
uv add "attaviz[tables]"
# or
pip install "attaviz[tables]"
```

Tables work without calling `attaviz.enable()`.

## Create your first table

Start with one row per observation and keep numbers numeric. These illustrative
observations include a missing completion rate to show how missing data appears.
The final `table` expression displays the result in a notebook or Quarto page.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import attaviz

participation = pd.DataFrame({
    "country": ["Indonesia", "Malaysia", "Philippines"],
    "participants": [12345, 8900, 6750],
    "completion": [0.876, 0.923, None],
    "funding": [1250000, 920000, 740000],
})

table = attaviz.table(
    participation,
    title="Program participation by country",
    subtitle="Illustrative counts, completion rates, and funding",
    source="Source: illustrative example data. N/A indicates unavailable data.",
)
table
```

The table preserves row order and numeric precision. Missing cells display as
`N/A`; numeric columns align right and text columns align left. Include the
“Source:” prefix yourself. Tables use their own title, subtitle, and source
arguments; the chart `frame()` helper does not apply to tables.

## Format counts, percentages, and currency

Use the original column names in formatting methods, even after changing their
display labels with `cols_label()`:

```{python}
formatted = (
    table
    .cols_label(
        country="Country",
        participants="Participants",
        completion="Completion",
        funding="Funding (USD)",
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns="participants")
    .fmt_percent(columns="completion", decimals=1)
    .fmt_currency(columns="funding", currency="USD", decimals=0)
)
formatted
```

The first row now shows `12,345`, `87.6%`, and `$1,250,000`. Percent formatting
expects fractions: store `0.876` for `87.6%`. If your data already contains
`87.6`, use `.fmt_percent(columns="completion", decimals=1, scale_values=False)`.
For ordinary decimal values, use `.fmt_number(columns="column_name", decimals=1)`.

These methods change the display while retaining the underlying values. D3
number/date strings are for Altair charts; use Great Tables formatting methods
for tables.

## Keep related columns close

Tables size to their content instead of stretching across the page. Put the
record identifier first and related measures next to each other. Use native
`cols_width()` to give longer labels enough room while keeping numeric columns
compact. Headers and body text wrap without ellipses or hover-only disclosure:

```{python}
formatted.cols_label(
    completion="Completed the program (%)",
).cols_width(
    country="150px",
    participants="120px",
    completion="140px",
    funding="140px",
)
```

Give each column enough room for its longest formatted value. Setting every
column width in pixels fixes the table to those widths; headers can still wrap.
A narrow page scrolls the table horizontally instead of hiding data.
For a table that should fill its container, use
`formatted.tab_options(table_width="100%")`.

## Row density and wide tables

The default uses 6 px vertical cell padding, 9 px horizontal padding, and 1.5
line height. Wrapped body text aligns to the top, and column headings follow the
same horizontal alignment as their values. Open Sans and tabular numerals keep
numeric columns readable without switching fonts.

Use subtle striping when it helps readers follow a row across many columns.
`opt_row_striping()` uses Attaviz's light grey. This example removes the internal
horizontal rules so the table uses one main row-tracking aid:

```{python}
wide_data = participation.assign(
    eligible=[18000, 12000, 9500],
    duration_months=[12, 18, 12],
)[["country", "eligible", "participants", "completion", "duration_months", "funding"]]

wide_table = (
    attaviz.table(
        wide_data,
        title="Program coverage and results",
        subtitle="Illustrative participation, completion, duration, and funding",
        source="Source: illustrative example data. N/A indicates unavailable data.",
    )
    .cols_label(
        country="Country",
        eligible="Eligible people",
        participants="Participants",
        completion="Completion (%)",
        duration_months="Duration (months)",
        funding="Funding (USD)",
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns=["eligible", "participants", "duration_months"])
    .fmt_percent(columns="completion", decimals=1)
    .fmt_currency(columns="funding", currency="USD", decimals=0)
    .opt_row_striping()
    .tab_options(table_body_hlines_style="none")
)
wide_table
```

Keep the default light rules for smaller tables. You can adjust density with
native `.tab_options(data_row_padding="9px")` when wrapped text needs more room;
rows grow with their content rather than being forced to a fixed height.

## Group columns and explain a value

Add a spanner above related columns and a footnote on the completion heading:

```{python}
from great_tables import loc

publication_table = (
    formatted
    .tab_spanner(label="Program results", columns=["participants", "completion"])
    .tab_footnote(
        "Completion is the share of participants who finished the program.",
        locations=loc.column_labels(columns="completion"),
    )
)
publication_table
```

Use `loc.body(columns="completion", rows=[2])` instead to attach a footnote to
the third row's completion cell. Great Tables uses zero-based row positions.

## Prepare row order and index labels

Sort or filter the DataFrame before passing it to `table()`. The DataFrame index
is omitted; if it contains labels you need, turn it into a column first:

```{python}
ranked = participation.set_index("country").sort_values("participants", ascending=False)

attaviz.table(
    ranked.reset_index(),
    title="Countries ordered by participation",
).fmt_integer(columns="participants")
```

## Export and share

To save the completed table, run these commands in your notebook or script:

```python
publication_table.write_raw_html("participation.html", make_page=True)
```

HTML export creates a standalone page and needs no browser. You can also get
HTML as a string with `publication_table.as_raw_html()` for embedding in another
page.

For image or PDF output:

```python
publication_table.gtsave("participation.png")
publication_table.gtsave("participation.pdf")
```

Image and PDF export use headless Chrome through Great Tables' `nokap`
dependency. See the [Great Tables export guide](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/user-guide/exporting-and-saving.html)
for environment setup.

## API and defaults

```python
attaviz.table(data, *, title=None, subtitle=None, source=None)
```

- `data` must be a non-empty pandas DataFrame with unique string column names.
  Attaviz copies it, preserving row order and omitting the index.
- `title`, `subtitle`, and `source` are optional plain text. A subtitle requires
  a title. Titles, subtitles, source notes, column names, and unformatted text
  cells are escaped as plain text.
- Styling uses Attaviz's medium typography and spacing, dark text on white,
  left-aligned headings, content-based widths, wrapping text, and subtle horizontal
  rules. Quarto table processing is disabled to preserve these defaults when
  embedding the table in documentation. Open Sans must be available
  in the viewing environment for an exact font match; otherwise a sans-serif
  fallback is used.

The WBG guide supplies the typography and colors; horizontal rules and other
table layout choices are Attaviz defaults. These are static publication tables;
sorting and pagination are outside this helper's defaults.

See the [table gallery](../gallery.qmd#tables) for more rendered examples.
